html:
FESTAC 77, the Second World Black and African Festival of Arts and Culture, was a month-long festival held in Lagos, Nigeria, in early 1977. Around 16,000 artists and performers came from dozens of countries in Africa and the African diaspora.

It followed a first festival held in Dakar in 1966, hosted by Léopold Sédar Senghor. Nigeria, rich from the oil boom of the 1970s and under military rule, spent heavily to make Lagos the capital of the black world. It built the National Theatre and a new housing estate, Festac Town, for the visitors.

There was music, dance, drama, film, art, literature and a colloquium on black culture and education. The emblem was the ivory mask of Queen Idia of Benin. Britain refused to lend the original, which British soldiers had taken in 1897 with the Benin Bronzes, and that refusal became a symbol of the fight to return looted art.

FESTAC was a high point of Pan-African cultural pride, though critics said its cost was a sign of oil-money waste.
